pullQuote: With Ouro UI, an agent can prepare a sharing action, but it can’t relabel the button or remove the confirmation.
testimonial: I’d choose Ouro UI because I want the button a person sees and the tool an agent calls to agree about what will happen. Its one action model generates both from a declaration, and `compare-mcp` checks what the running server actually advertises. The `ActionButton` validator rejects a generated card that disguises “Share recipe” as “Add to list.” Flutter would let me maintain one UI implementation across platforms; with Ouro, I’d take on separate native kits and test the Android flow on hardware before shipping.
evaluations:
**A2UI** — My pick for a portable *wire format*. Its [SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) negotiate catalogs and apply updates by component ID, so changing one part of a form needn’t cost the user focus in another. Its [function rules](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/) distinguish remote callers from functions requiring a user gesture. A gesture alone doesn’t establish that a button accurately describes the action. I’d pair A2UI with trusted action labels and reviewed confirmation screens, and negotiate versions: the documented Compose renderer supports 0.9.1, not all the 1.0 rules.

**Flutter** — A [single Dart widget implementation](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) can serve mobile, desktop and web, with Material and Cupertino controls and platform channels for OS integration. The [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui) goes beyond chat: it builds from a widget catalog and feeds interaction state back to the agent, though the package is marked alpha. I’d prefer Flutter if sharing the whole screen implementation were paramount; I’d still define callable business operations and approval rules independently of widget state.

**Radix UI** — `asChild` can put both dialog and tooltip behavior on one real button rather than nesting interactive elements. The [composition guide](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition) also identifies exactly how a custom trigger can break: drop its ref or props, or replace it with a non-focusable element. I’d use Radix for the web controls, test the composed triggers with a keyboard, and expose the underlying actions separately rather than ask an agent to operate dialogs.

**json-render** — `defineCatalog` describes components and actions, `defineRegistry` binds them to implementations, and SpecStream progressively applies model output. The [renderer examples](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render) cover React Native as well as web, even PDF and terminal output. That breadth is excellent for a reporting product. For an editable or consequential workflow, I’d constrain the relationship between label and action as well as their individual types: the example Button accepts both as strings. I’d also authorize the handler regardless of whether a press or a state watcher triggered it.

**Ouro UI** — The deciding evidence was a [validator test](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/a8d6c3076a342bfcede72d874de9354dcaa4e2fa/test/composed.test.mts) that changes a share button’s label, removes its confirmation, and tries to supply input to a person-only order; each change is rejected. The [action generator](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) also checks generated files and the live MCP tool list for drift. These checks complement, rather than replace, authorization in the handlers. The [platform matrix](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md) distinguishes native tree rendering on all four targets from A2UI ingestion on web and Apple. I’d pilot on actual devices: the [Android kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) documents eight standalone controls and emulator-only testing; the [Windows kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) has not verified agent discovery on a Windows client.

**MCP Apps** — The [specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx) links a tool to a `ui://` HTML resource; a sandboxed iframe communicates with the host over JSON-RPC. I’d use that to deliver an interactive chart across compatible chat clients without rebuilding it for each one. The portable artifact is a web view, not a native widget tree, and extension support is negotiated. I’d keep the tool useful without the view and provide a native renderer where host controls matter.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) gives me adaptive controls and model-driven views; the [HIG](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines) guides choices such as layout and input conventions. [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) makes this a serious agent-facing option too: named actions and entities become discoverable to Siri and Shortcuts without anyone navigating a screen. I’d choose it directly for Apple-only delivery. For the broader brief, I want the same operation defined for a web tool and Android client without keeping three declarations in sync.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — The [UI library](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) supplies Radix-based React components and Tailwind 4 tokens matched to ChatGPT. That solves a concrete problem: a reservation card can look and behave like part of the host. The [integration guide](https://developers.openai.com/apps-sdk/build/chatgpt-ui/) separates those optional components from the MCP Apps bridge and recommends keeping tools usable without UI. I’d follow that separation for ChatGPT distribution, not adopt this host’s styling as the foundation for standalone native screens.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The [architecture](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum/blob/main/rfcs/2019-v3-architecture.md) separates platform-independent state, interaction hooks and themed components. That lets me keep keyboard, focus and internationalization behavior when replacing the visual design, a strong reason to use it for complex web inputs. Reusable selection state, however, doesn’t tell an agent what selecting a record permits it to do. I’d put these controls behind a web renderer and bind them to the same domain actions as the native views.

**Tamagui** — Its [optional compiler](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/compiler-install) can flatten styled JSX into DOM and CSS on web or plain React Native views on mobile. That’s a practical way for one team to share screens, themes and variants without requiring every styling abstraction to survive at runtime. I’d choose it for a React/React Native product with an existing tool API. For this brief I’d have to supply the connection from that API to the controls, including when a person must confirm.

**AI Elements** — I’d use its presentation patterns for a conversation: Message Scroller keeps the reader’s place, Trace groups tool activity, and Confirmation gives a person an approval affordance. The original [repository](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) announces its move; the [shadcn migration guide](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements) explains that existing copies still work and identifies patterns without replacements. For new work I’d use the successor patterns. Drawing a confirmation prompt is useful, but the backend must refuse execution without approval, including from clients that don’t display chat.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — The closest competitor on shared business operations. Its [action layer](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) routes UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A and CLI calls through the same server implementation, validation, access checks and audit trail. I’d prefer that design for a TypeScript workspace where the hard problem is synchronizing people and agents around shared records. For native delivery I favor Ouro’s generated system actions and checked button labels; I’d otherwise budget for binding native controls to Builder’s excellent backend contract.

**Vercel UI SDK** — This beta goes beyond helping agents *write* components. Its [browser bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/reference) exposes `snapshot`, `query` and `act`; an `allow` callback can refuse a resolved action, and a marked confirmation fails without approval. The [behavior core](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui) serves five web adapters. I’d use it when the task really is editing what’s on the page. An off-page component has no available actions, though, so I’d give durable operations their own API rather than make them depend on a mounted control.

**CopilotKit** — AG-UI carries events between an existing agent and the frontend, with shared state, A2UI and MCP Apps support in the [stack](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit). Its [human-in-the-loop guide](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/human-in-the-loop) makes an important distinction: the model chooses whether to ask via `useHumanInTheLoop`, whereas backend code can require a pause via an interrupt. I’d choose it for a collaborative copilot, use an enforced checkpoint for mandatory approval, and verify backend support: the guide notes interrupts are temporarily unavailable on the Built-in Agent. I’d still want a common action definition for entry points outside the conversation.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Android’s [MaterialTheme](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) propagates color, typography and shape to composables and can adapt colors to the user’s wallpaper. [AppFunctions](https://developer.android.com/ai/appfunctions) lets authorized callers discover and execute app operations on-device; Google marks the API experimental. I’d use both for an Android-first product and test discovery on the supported OS versions. Neither Android theming nor OS registration is a shared declaration for my web and Apple clients.

**Base UI** — Its [composition contract](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition) specifies how `render` merges classes, styles, handlers and refs onto one element, including which handler can stop subsequent ones. That precision matters when a branded toolbar button also opens a menu. I’d choose it for a custom React design system. I wouldn’t use merged click-handler order as a business permission check; native and agent callers need an operation that enforces the rule independently of the React tree.

**Fluent UI** — The [web project](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui) offers distinct React v9, v8 and Web Component implementations, including a gradual migration path for Office-style apps. The separate [React Native library](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-react-native) explicitly calls its targets alpha and documents per-control platform differences. I’d use Fluent where Microsoft product consistency matters, but verify the required controls on each device rather than assume visual parity implies behavioral parity. I’d keep tool definitions shared outside those component packages.

**MUI** — [Material UI](https://github.com/mui/material-ui) pairs a comprehensive React implementation of Material Design with MUI X for complex controls, a persuasive starting point for a data-heavy web console. Its [MCP server](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/) supplies official documentation and examples to coding assistants; that is different from exposing the console’s own operations to an end-user agent. I’d reuse MUI on web and put record selection and mutation behind a typed service shared with native clients.

**Chakra UI** — Its [React component system](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui) offers accessible styled controls, and the [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server) let a coding agent look up actual component props, examples and theme tokens rather than guess. That’s a useful authoring advantage, not a runtime contract for actions in the finished app. I’d use Chakra to implement web views for a team already using it, with a separate action catalog for agent and native access.

**shadcn/ui** — Its [registry](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry) distributes source files, including hooks, pages and rules, and isn’t restricted to React. That gives a team ownership of its controls and gives coding agents inspectable examples. It also means two applications can install the same button and later change what it does independently. I’d use the registry for distribution, then share action schemas and run conformance checks on the installed implementations rather than treat common source ancestry as a runtime guarantee.

actions.pullQuote: With Ouro UI, an agent can prepare a sharing action, but it can’t relabel the button or remove the confirmation.
actions.testimonial: I’d choose Ouro UI because I want the button a person sees and the tool an agent calls to agree about what will happen. Its one action model generates both from a declaration, and `compare-mcp` checks what the running server actually advertises. The `ActionButton` validator rejects a generated card that disguises “Share recipe” as “Add to list.” Flutter would let me maintain one UI implementation across platforms; with Ouro, I’d take on separate native kits and test the Android flow on hardware before shipping.
actions.evaluations:
**A2UI** — My pick for a portable *wire format*. Its [SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) negotiate catalogs and apply updates by component ID, so changing one part of a form needn’t cost the user focus in another. Its [function rules](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/) distinguish remote callers from functions requiring a user gesture. A gesture alone doesn’t establish that a button accurately describes the action. I’d pair A2UI with trusted action labels and reviewed confirmation screens, and negotiate versions: the documented Compose renderer supports 0.9.1, not all the 1.0 rules.

**Flutter** — A [single Dart widget implementation](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) can serve mobile, desktop and web, with Material and Cupertino controls and platform channels for OS integration. The [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui) goes beyond chat: it builds from a widget catalog and feeds interaction state back to the agent, though the package is marked alpha. I’d prefer Flutter if sharing the whole screen implementation were paramount; I’d still define callable business operations and approval rules independently of widget state.

**Radix UI** — `asChild` can put both dialog and tooltip behavior on one real button rather than nesting interactive elements. The [composition guide](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition) also identifies exactly how a custom trigger can break: drop its ref or props, or replace it with a non-focusable element. I’d use Radix for the web controls, test the composed triggers with a keyboard, and expose the underlying actions separately rather than ask an agent to operate dialogs.

**json-render** — `defineCatalog` describes components and actions, `defineRegistry` binds them to implementations, and SpecStream progressively applies model output. The [renderer examples](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render) cover React Native as well as web, even PDF and terminal output. That breadth is excellent for a reporting product. For an editable or consequential workflow, I’d constrain the relationship between label and action as well as their individual types: the example Button accepts both as strings. I’d also authorize the handler regardless of whether a press or a state watcher triggered it.

**Ouro UI** — The deciding evidence was a [validator test](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/a8d6c3076a342bfcede72d874de9354dcaa4e2fa/test/composed.test.mts) that changes a share button’s label, removes its confirmation, and tries to supply input to a person-only order; each change is rejected. The [action generator](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) also checks generated files and the live MCP tool list for drift. These checks complement, rather than replace, authorization in the handlers. The [platform matrix](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md) distinguishes native tree rendering on all four targets from A2UI ingestion on web and Apple. I’d pilot on actual devices: the [Android kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) documents eight standalone controls and emulator-only testing; the [Windows kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) has not verified agent discovery on a Windows client.

**MCP Apps** — The [specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx) links a tool to a `ui://` HTML resource; a sandboxed iframe communicates with the host over JSON-RPC. I’d use that to deliver an interactive chart across compatible chat clients without rebuilding it for each one. The portable artifact is a web view, not a native widget tree, and extension support is negotiated. I’d keep the tool useful without the view and provide a native renderer where host controls matter.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) gives me adaptive controls and model-driven views; the [HIG](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines) guides choices such as layout and input conventions. [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) makes this a serious agent-facing option too: named actions and entities become discoverable to Siri and Shortcuts without anyone navigating a screen. I’d choose it directly for Apple-only delivery. For the broader brief, I want the same operation defined for a web tool and Android client without keeping three declarations in sync.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — The [UI library](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) supplies Radix-based React components and Tailwind 4 tokens matched to ChatGPT. That solves a concrete problem: a reservation card can look and behave like part of the host. The [integration guide](https://developers.openai.com/apps-sdk/build/chatgpt-ui/) separates those optional components from the MCP Apps bridge and recommends keeping tools usable without UI. I’d follow that separation for ChatGPT distribution, not adopt this host’s styling as the foundation for standalone native screens.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The [architecture](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum/blob/main/rfcs/2019-v3-architecture.md) separates platform-independent state, interaction hooks and themed components. That lets me keep keyboard, focus and internationalization behavior when replacing the visual design, a strong reason to use it for complex web inputs. Reusable selection state, however, doesn’t tell an agent what selecting a record permits it to do. I’d put these controls behind a web renderer and bind them to the same domain actions as the native views.

**Tamagui** — Its [optional compiler](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/compiler-install) can flatten styled JSX into DOM and CSS on web or plain React Native views on mobile. That’s a practical way for one team to share screens, themes and variants without requiring every styling abstraction to survive at runtime. I’d choose it for a React/React Native product with an existing tool API. For this brief I’d have to supply the connection from that API to the controls, including when a person must confirm.

**AI Elements** — I’d use its presentation patterns for a conversation: Message Scroller keeps the reader’s place, Trace groups tool activity, and Confirmation gives a person an approval affordance. The original [repository](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) announces its move; the [shadcn migration guide](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements) explains that existing copies still work and identifies patterns without replacements. For new work I’d use the successor patterns. Drawing a confirmation prompt is useful, but the backend must refuse execution without approval, including from clients that don’t display chat.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — The closest competitor on shared business operations. Its [action layer](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) routes UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A and CLI calls through the same server implementation, validation, access checks and audit trail. I’d prefer that design for a TypeScript workspace where the hard problem is synchronizing people and agents around shared records. For native delivery I favor Ouro’s generated system actions and checked button labels; I’d otherwise budget for binding native controls to Builder’s excellent backend contract.

**Vercel UI SDK** — This beta goes beyond helping agents *write* components. Its [browser bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/reference) exposes `snapshot`, `query` and `act`; an `allow` callback can refuse a resolved action, and a marked confirmation fails without approval. The [behavior core](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui) serves five web adapters. I’d use it when the task really is editing what’s on the page. An off-page component has no available actions, though, so I’d give durable operations their own API rather than make them depend on a mounted control.

**CopilotKit** — AG-UI carries events between an existing agent and the frontend, with shared state, A2UI and MCP Apps support in the [stack](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit). Its [human-in-the-loop guide](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/human-in-the-loop) makes an important distinction: the model chooses whether to ask via `useHumanInTheLoop`, whereas backend code can require a pause via an interrupt. I’d choose it for a collaborative copilot, use an enforced checkpoint for mandatory approval, and verify backend support: the guide notes interrupts are temporarily unavailable on the Built-in Agent. I’d still want a common action definition for entry points outside the conversation.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Android’s [MaterialTheme](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) propagates color, typography and shape to composables and can adapt colors to the user’s wallpaper. [AppFunctions](https://developer.android.com/ai/appfunctions) lets authorized callers discover and execute app operations on-device; Google marks the API experimental. I’d use both for an Android-first product and test discovery on the supported OS versions. Neither Android theming nor OS registration is a shared declaration for my web and Apple clients.

**Base UI** — Its [composition contract](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition) specifies how `render` merges classes, styles, handlers and refs onto one element, including which handler can stop subsequent ones. That precision matters when a branded toolbar button also opens a menu. I’d choose it for a custom React design system. I wouldn’t use merged click-handler order as a business permission check; native and agent callers need an operation that enforces the rule independently of the React tree.

**Fluent UI** — The [web project](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui) offers distinct React v9, v8 and Web Component implementations, including a gradual migration path for Office-style apps. The separate [React Native library](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-react-native) explicitly calls its targets alpha and documents per-control platform differences. I’d use Fluent where Microsoft product consistency matters, but verify the required controls on each device rather than assume visual parity implies behavioral parity. I’d keep tool definitions shared outside those component packages.

**MUI** — [Material UI](https://github.com/mui/material-ui) pairs a comprehensive React implementation of Material Design with MUI X for complex controls, a persuasive starting point for a data-heavy web console. Its [MCP server](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/) supplies official documentation and examples to coding assistants; that is different from exposing the console’s own operations to an end-user agent. I’d reuse MUI on web and put record selection and mutation behind a typed service shared with native clients.

**Chakra UI** — Its [React component system](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui) offers accessible styled controls, and the [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server) let a coding agent look up actual component props, examples and theme tokens rather than guess. That’s a useful authoring advantage, not a runtime contract for actions in the finished app. I’d use Chakra to implement web views for a team already using it, with a separate action catalog for agent and native access.

**shadcn/ui** — Its [registry](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry) distributes source files, including hooks, pages and rules, and isn’t restricted to React. That gives a team ownership of its controls and gives coding agents inspectable examples. It also means two applications can install the same button and later change what it does independently. I’d use the registry for distribution, then share action schemas and run conformance checks on the installed implementations rather than treat common source ancestry as a runtime guarantee.
